prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level of systematic uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (Katori and Ye) as my single-part position, and the second round has made me firmer, not merely unchanged. The chair asks which criterion should decide between B061 and B013. Mine is this: a Nobel Prize in physics should reward a discovery or invention whose central claim is complete, reproduced and exactly attributable today. B061 meets all three. The invention has a definite form, a neutral-atom lattice at the magic wavelength that cancels the first-order light shift while removing Doppler and recoil effects. Its performance has been reproduced and compared across several laboratories, and the 10^-18 level is established by systematic-uncertainty budgets that other groups can audit. I value that as an experimentalist who has to defend the reliability of a measurement, not a story about it. I also think the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems do not cover this. They honoured a tool for reading optical frequencies and the manipulation of individual ions, not a neutral-atom ensemble clock whose accuracy depends on lattice-induced shifts. A citation worded narrowly on the lattice clock, and silent on ion-clock priority, answers the chair's first question. On attribution I split the credit as follows: Katori for the concept and the first demonstration of the magic-wavelength lattice, Ye for taking the system to its limiting accuracy and stability, including the many-body regime. That split is not arbitrary, and I will say below why I now consider it defensible. I did not move to a two-part configuration. The only part I could pair with B061 inside the three-person cap would be a single-name part, and none of those has the maturity or support to justify it. I rely on my recollection of the history, not on checked sources.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my position is the one B013 supporters make, and it is a serious one: B013 opens a new regime of correlated matter, whereas B061 is a higher level of precision. If the committee's criterion is breadth of new physics, B013 is probably the larger result, and I do not claim otherwise. My answer is that the prize has often honoured instruments and measurements as well as discoveries of new states, and that completeness and clean credit are legitimate tie-breakers when two candidates are close. There are real weaknesses in B061 as well. Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will look like repetition to some readers, however distinct the physics. The credit leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and ion-clock pioneers; any two-name allocation is a judgement and not a unique answer. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the consequence is still prospective. I would accept that a committee which weighed novelty of regime over completeness could reasonably choose B013 and I would then want Bistritzer kept in the credit set.

responses.point: Rests the case for B061 on atomic-structure physics she can judge directly (magic-wavelength polarisabilities, blackbody-radiation shift) and treats the 2005 and 2012 prizes as distinct, while noting that credit extends to Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, PTB and SYRTE.
responses.response: My round-1 question to you was how the committee should treat those other groups, and I read your statement as an answer of a kind: the physics that makes the clock work, the magic wavelength and the control of the blackbody shift, is Katori's concept and Ye's demonstration, and the others contributed to its confirmation and refinement. That is a reasonable basis for a two-name split, not only convention. Where I would ask you to be more explicit is the 10^-18 milestone. If you, as the atomic-structure expert, regard it as belonging to a wider group, then the citation should rest on the invention and its realisation, not on the milestone itself. I have written my citation that way, with the figure attached to the realisation and not to a named priority claim.

responses.point: Calls the lattice clock a distinct successor to the 2005 comb and 2012 single-system prizes and notes that the practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, has not happened yet and may make this a better candidate next year than this year.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness. I disagree that waiting is the safer course. The Nobel criterion is a discovery or invention, not a completed standards decision, and the invention and its performance are already demonstrated, reproduced and compared. A prize that waited for the redefinition of the second would make a metrological decision the condition for a physics judgement. I also see a risk in waiting: the credit set becomes harder to hold at two names as more groups report at the 10^-18 level. I do accept your point that the redefinition will make the practical consequence vivid. I would mention the pending redefinition in the scientific background, not in the citation.

responses.point: Argues that Bistritzer must stay in a B013 credit set because he led the 2011 continuum-model prediction, and that my attribution worry about Knut Urban in B056 is of the same kind as the one I raise for moire; he also doubts a Hosono-only credit for iron pnictides.
responses.response: On B013 we agree, and I would hold that line if the committee prefers it: dropping Bistritzer would sever the prediction that gives the prize its shape. On B056, you are right that it carries an attribution problem, and I am recused from deciding it, so I only note that the observation does not change my ballot. On iron pnictides I accept your correction. Chen and Zhao drove the key increase in transition temperature and a Hosono-only credit does not describe the field, which is one more reason that B012 is not in my configuration. Your point on Urban in B056 and mine on Cao in B013 show that the three-name cap is hard for both candidates, which is why I think attribution should be a tie-breaker between close candidates and not the decisive criterion.

responses.point: Argues that B013 pairs a quantitative prediction with an experimental result nobody demanded of nature, that it is reproduced by many groups, and that it has the broadest conceptual reach on the shortlist; also that the credit problem for Cao and Fatemi is a hard but acceptable consequence of the three-person limit.
responses.response: Your argument on breadth is the strongest one against my position, and I do not dismiss it. I am not persuaded on the maturity side. The correlated insulators are reproduced and the platform is real, but the interpretation of the superconducting phase and several correlated states is still moving, and the decisive experimental paper carries a student first author who falls outside the three-name set. For B061 the claim is closed in the sense that matters for a prize, and the credit problem is smaller. I think the committee should state openly, as the chair's question suggests, which criterion decides. If it is novelty of regime, you are right. If it is a completed, reproduced claim with clean credit, B061 wins. I stay with the second.

responses.point: Calls twisted bilayer graphene a rare case where calculation anticipated a qualitatively new regime and experiment confirmed it, and suggests that a prize could be built from MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero alone.
responses.response: I maintain what I said in round 1: the prediction and the experiment belong together, and a MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero pair removes the first author of the continuum-model paper, which would weaken the case. If the committee chose B013 I would support the three listed names with an explicit statement about Cao and Fatemi. I also read your own file as saying that B061 is the cleaner allocation, and I think that is the heart of the question: B013 is probably the bigger result, B061 the more finished one. For this year I weigh finished more heavily.

responses.point: Keeps Cirac and Zoller first for conceptual originality and clean two-name credit, while conceding that B013 and B061 have broader support and that the citation must be drawn narrowly to avoid the ion and cold-atom experimental record.
responses.response: I respect that you present your preference as a judgement on originality and not a vote count. My difficulty remains that the prize would honour the blueprint while the experiments that proved it, ion-trap gates and cold-atom simulation, are recognised in part in 2012 and 2022 or lie outside the credit set. You have not yet said what would make B034 preferable to B061 or B013 on attribution and maturity, which the chair also asks. I would be willing to move if the citation could be drawn so narrowly on the proposals that it does not depend on those experiments, but I do not see how that is done without making the achievement smaller.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the 2005 and 2012 prizes as having already honoured lattice clocks, in which case B061 would look like repetition regardless of the physics.

Whether the split of credit between Katori (concept, first demonstration) and Ye (limiting accuracy and many-body regime) can withstand scrutiny against the work of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; I am working from recollection of the history.
Whether the committee prefers novelty of regime (B013) to completeness and clean credit (B061) as the deciding criterion, and whether it will state that criterion openly.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this year or a later year the better time for B061.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene is a timing issue or only a matter of citation wording.
statement.conflict_note: I remain recused from deciding B056 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy), which lies in my own research field of transmission electron microscopy and the international microscopy community where I hold a leadership role. I have not put it in my preferred configuration or among my alternatives. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie to any credited name in B061, B013 or B019. My work on oxide interfaces (the lanthanum-aluminate/strontium-titanate system) is a different materials system from twisted bilayer graphene and topological insulators. The Chalmers connection with Goran Johansson does not touch B061, B013, B019 or B034, and he has said that he would recuse himself from B018, which I do not propose.
